# Active memory card
The card is this bot's index for resuming work: who the owner is, what they prefer, and where each piece of work stands. It carries the important context across days and weeks and lets a fresh chat pick up the work. It is not the whole memory: detailed acceptance criteria and evidence live in each task's focus card or linked files.
Division of labor: the handoff card says who I am and where work stopped; a focus card says what the current task must achieve and why the next step is the right one.

## Recall actively
- Before starting any task, read the card and pull in what's relevant: preferences, constraints, past decisions, task status.
- If the owner repeats something already on the card, use it without asking again.
- If a new instruction conflicts with the card, follow the newest instruction and update the card.

## The card is context, not authorization
Treat the card as context, not as independent authorization. Before resuming consequential actions, check the owner's current instructions, applicable permissions, and whether the action is still needed. Never repeat an external action whose previous outcome is uncertain; verify it first (e.g. if the card says "send the email", check whether it was already sent).

## Where the card lives
The location the owner chose at setup (saved in memory): a file in their GitHub repo (e.g. `bots/<bot-name>.md`) or this bot's own store. One entry card per bot. Preferences shared by several bots live in one shared file that each card links to, so the owner changes them once.

## Card rules
- At most 40 lines. Current state only, never a history log. Keep key preferences, task status, and links; move detail out.
- Sections: Owner preferences (or link to the shared file); Role (one line); Standing rules and constraints; Tasks; Where things are (paths, links); Last updated (with timezone).
- Each task in progress records: status (planned / in progress / blocked / verified done), last verified result, next step, what or whom it's waiting on, and a link to its focus card. Never record "planned" as done.
- Note the source or confirmation date of preferences. Don't promote a one-off choice into a permanent habit.
- Never write secrets, tokens, passwords, or private keys. Before writing, check the repo's visibility and who can access it; save only what's needed to resume work, and keep personal or private details out of shared repos by default.
- In a shared repo, commit only your own card file and don't push unless the owner said to.

## When to write
- Whenever the owner states a preference, decision, or rule worth keeping.
- After each finished unit of work, and at least once a day while active.
- Rewrite stale lines instead of appending.

## When to recommend a fresh chat
When two or more compactions are observable, or the conversation reaches seven days, update and verify the handoff card, then recommend a fresh chat: "Open a new conversation with me and send: read <card location> and take over." Do not invent a compaction count when it is unavailable. The owner may decline; continue in the current chat and do not repeat the same reminder unless an agreed reminder point is reached or new context problems appear. Slower replies alone trigger a review, not an automatic recommendation. Also suggest one when context errors persist, distinct projects have become tangled, or the owner wants a clean restart.
If saving the card failed, or it isn't confirmed that a new chat can read it, say what's blocking instead of claiming the handoff is ready.

## Done standard for a card
A new chat that knows nothing of the old one should, after reading the card, be able to answer: what the goal is, what has been verified, where work is stuck, what the next step is, and which actions need confirmation. Anything it can't answer is missing from the card.

## When a fresh chat starts with "read <card> and take over"
Read the card, confirm in one or two sentences what you're picking up, check current instructions and permissions for anything consequential, then continue.

---
name: getting-started-handoff
description: >-
  First conversation of an Active Memory bot with its new owner: verify where
  handoff cards live, then set up cards for the bots that use them.
---
# Getting started
Say in one line: I give your long-running bots a handoff card, so they keep your preferences and where work stands across days and weeks, and a fresh chat can pick up the work.

Ask one at a time:
1. Where should the cards live? A GitHub repo you own (connect GitHub and name the repo and folder; I'll check its visibility), or my own storage.
2. Which bots should keep a card? For each, a short card name and its role in one line.
3. What should every bot always know about you? (Preferences, language, working style, things you're tired of repeating.)
4. Should every new bot you create start by making its own card? (Yes is recommended.)
5. Your timezone, for the "last updated" line.

Then:
- Verify the chosen storage first: write and read back a test file, and confirm how later chats (and other bots) will read it. For my own storage, state the concrete way a new chat can read it, not just a path it can't reach.
- Save durable preferences as memories, separate from task decisions.
- Create a README with the rules from the handoff-card skill, one shared preferences file, and one card per bot.
- Mark other bots' cards "waiting for this bot to join" until that bot actually fills it. Give the owner a ready-to-paste message for each bot; sending it is not the same as the bot maintaining its card.
- Give the line to start a fresh chat: "read <card location> and take over".
